utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Carmela Javier, Barney Thomas, Salvatore Cannata, and Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see a brand new team from Defence. Good morning. Could we have appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. Good morning, Your Honour. Gregor Guy-Smith, Chad Mair, and Tina Drolec on behalf of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just before we call Mr. Guy-Smith, last week the last witness we -- a document was tendered through him XN195 which became P2914 which was supposed to be MFI'd pending translation, and I forgot to mention that it must be MFI'd. May the record show that that exhibit is marked for identification. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. With the Court's permission, our next witness will be Mr. Jevdjevic, and he will be led by Mr. Chad Mair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Could you please state your whole name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And I know you've testified here several times previously and I think you're pretty familiar as to how this works, so we'll just go ahead and get started. Could you start by stating where you were born and when, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 11th of December, 1963, in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And what country is Rogatica in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Have you lived in Rogatica your entire life?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Rogatica during the first 14 years of my life, that is to say, until I completed elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: After you turned 14, where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After elementary school, I completed the military high school in Belgrade and the military academy of the land forces, the signals department, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When did you complete the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What rank did you graduate with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: After you completed the military academy, what did you do following that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I was transferred to the garrison of the Yugoslav People's Army in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in Uzice for five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when you left Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was sent with a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army to carry out assignments in the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the present-day territory of the Republic of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What was your position within the unit that you went to the Republika Srpska Krajina with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was commander of the signals battalion of the 1st Operations Group that covered part of the theatre of war in the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When did you go to the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long did you remain on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained there until the beginning of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that point an order arrived that the Yugoslav People's Army should withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina after the UNPROFOR units arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you remember who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that that order was issued by the Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you ever see that order or did you just hear about it -- sorry, let me back up. Did you hear about the order at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you see the order at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could call up D242 on the e-court screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You can see in the upper left-hand corner it says the federal secretariat of national defence, office of the federal secretary, strictly confidential number 5-34, 6 May 1992. Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to see this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Is this the order that you believe you're referring to regarding the JNA withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English and I believe the bottom of the B/C/S page. Page 2 in the B/C/S as well I think. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And can you see there who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The order was issued by the Chief of General Staff, Colonel-General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, if we could go back to the first page in each of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, do you remember when you were made aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said, sometime in the beginning of May 1992, the commander of that unit that I was serving in on that mission told us what the content of this order was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Excellent. And what did you do, if anything, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, I asked for the following possibility, to stay in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although the unit was withdrawing into the Republic of Serbia. Because I originally came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by then the civil war had already broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who did you ask for that -- the possibility to stay in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked the commander of that unit of the JNA that was in that part of the theatre of war in the Republic of Srpska Krajina and that was given the task of returning to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall what his response was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: He said that all officers who were born in the territory of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could, if they so wish, remain in the territory and join the units of their people who had already started organising themselves in certain units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I understand a little point. I thought you said your unit was in the Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army that was in the territory of the then- -- I mean it was sent from Serbia to the theatre of war in the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I was saying. But I see -- I haven't read through this entire order, but on the heading here, the first paragraph seems to refer to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this couldn't have been -- this couldn't refer to you in the RSK, could it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army at that period of time was given the assignment of withdrawing from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Now, whether it would stay in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or whether it would go directly to the territory of the Republic of Serbia is something that we did not know at that point in time. Simply, the JNA received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: You were in the RSK. This order applies to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It couldn't have been referring to you, to your unit, could it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander conveyed the content of this order to us. I had not seen this order, but he conveyed the content of the order to us, namely, that all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take it you're not able to answer my question. You may proceed, Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, when you left Croatia, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to Bosanska Krupa, to a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska that was being organised in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What country is Bosanska Krupa in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Bosanska Krupa is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Approximately when, if you recall, did you go to Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of the month of May, probably around the 4th or 5th or 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall if you went by yourself, did you go with a unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Four of us officers who were in that previous unit and who had been born in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina all went to that unit together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If you could focus your attention on paragraph 1, number 1, of the document on this screen, it's at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Perhaps we could scroll down a little bit on each. If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if I could just ask for your comment on paragraph 1 -- number 1, paragraph number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In order to carry out the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY dated the 5th of May, dealing with the further position of the Yugoslav People's Army in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say that the position of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was being looked into, and then the Supreme Command Staff looked at the status of active military personnel and civilians serving in the Yugoslav People's Army to whom the mentioned decision pertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could just clarify a couple of points that you just raised there. Who -- the Supreme Command Staff of which army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you got to Bosanska Krupa, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When we returned to Bosanska Krupa, we reported to the command of the brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska that had been established in Bosanska Krupa. Actually, this was a unit of the organised Serb people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you say "a unit of the organised Serb people in the area," who organised it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The people organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you know if they were part of a larger organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I know that they corresponded to other similar units of the Serb people in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You stated initially that it was a command of the brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska before you edited that. Were you aware of the Army of Republika Srpska? Had it been created at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I hadn't been aware of that particular formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall when the Army of Republika Srpska was created?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that was sometime in May, in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: About two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: While you were there, what were your duties -- we'll just start with that. What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was chief of signals for that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you -- were you part of a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there, the brigade commander was a reserve major. His name was Milan Sarac or Strbac. I can't remember his exact last name, Sarac or Strbac I think. So when they organised themselves, they appointed as commander this reserve major from that particular town. I know that when I arrived there or while I was there a colonel was appointed to that position who came together with us from that former JNA unit on which we served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- sir, you say this Sarac or Strbac was appointed as a commander and then you go on to say that a colonel was appointed to that position. To what position? And who is this colonel, this colonel who came together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his last name exactly, but that information can be found in files, dossiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but what position did -- was this colonel appointed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was appointed brigade commander. And the previous commander, reserve Major Sarac, was then appointed as his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you said that you were chief of signals for the brigade. How did you come to be in that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since that is my specialty, signals, it was most logical for me to carry out that duty in that brigade. The commander of that brigade gave me that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you say that he gave you that duty, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: He ordered me to carry out the duty of signals chief, and I started getting to know the units, the equipment, the plans, and the organisation of signals in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And just so there's no confusion, when you refer to "signals," what are you actually referring to? Can you just elaborate briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of the system of communications of command in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: The -- who's the brigade subordinated to, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The brigade was subordinated to the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, or, rather, that's what we considered it to be, the superior command, the command that was superior to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could just clarify that. I believe you said that the Army of Republika Srpska was not created until the second half of May. I think that you said you arrived here on the 6th of May. So between that time-period, do you -- who was that unit subordinated to, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was subordinated to the superior command which was in Bihac in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You said that you were in Bosanska Krupa for approximately two weeks. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After that, I asked the brigade commander to be transferred to the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in view of the fact that that is where my family was. I did not know what was going on with them in that war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What was the response of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: He told me that I could hand over duty to my deputy, and he allowed he me to go to the area where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And just so we're clear on the chronology, about when did you go to the eastern part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the eastern part of Bosnia in late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Where specifically did you go in the eastern part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I went to the Han Pijesak garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What was located at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The command post of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was in the vicinity of Han Pijesak, as was the signals unit, the 67th Signals Regiment, which served the needs of that staff, that headquarters, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who did you report to at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My superior officer was Lieutenant-Colonel Gvozden Bosko, who was the commander of the signals regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And I'll ask you the same question that I asked you before, how did you come to be in the -- actually, you don't know the answer to that. What position did you fill when you went to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the company leader of the radio company in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How did you come to be in that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by the commander of the signals regiment whom I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How large was your company, the radio company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It had some 30 to 40 men. That was the unit I was in command of and the equipment appropriate to the purpose of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just spend a moment on the structure of the unit there. Who did your company report to? Where did it fit in within the structure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was the radio company, the telephone/telegraph company, and the company for stationary communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And were those part of a larger unit? Were they off on their own?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: They were all part of a larger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What unit was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: They were part of a battalion which was part of the signals regiment of the army of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you undergo any sort of formal procedure or ceremony within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time you've just said that the battalion was part of the army of the Main Staff of the VRS. Did you -- you didn't simply just come there. Did you join the VRS? Was there any sort of -- any sort of procedure that -- to become part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On arrival, I reported to the regiment commander. He already had vacant posts which he needed to fill for the better functioning of his unit, so he issued an order appointing me company leader of the radio company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. We've covered that. But as far as joining the larger VRS, was there any sort of procedure, anything that you did, a ceremony, an oath, papers, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that on the Vidovdan holiday, the 28th of June, when the young generation of soldiers, the first generation of conscripts serving in the Army of Republika Srpska, together with all the commanding officers who were there, were lined up, and they took an oath to the Army of Republika Srpska. At that point in time, however, I was at Milici engaged in combat tasks, so I personally did not attend that ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did there ever come a point in time that you took the oath?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not, because I felt it was a pure formality, something that was nothing but protocol. And this was understood among us, my colleagues and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that it was nothing but protocol? Could you just elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the oath-taking ceremony is simply a ceremony, something to do with protocol. But what is stated in that oath was something that we had spoken to ourselves long before that ceremony, because we belonged to that army. There was no need to declare it officially and ceremoniously and solemnly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you know more specifically what the oath said, what was stated in the oath?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The text of the oath was the usual one that all armies use, and it's that we would defend the constitutional order and the territory of what was then called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you have to sign anything, to fill out any paperwork?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: All the soldiers taking the solemn oath sign a copy of the text that they had spoken. Due to pressing reasons of combat, I was unable to attend that ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: That's understood, but did you still sign the oath?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you receive anything from the VRS? Were you given anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I had a military booklet, a military ID card, that is, and all the duties and the -- everything that an officer was issued with: weapons, a uniform, an office, equipment, men, tasks, responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's break that down briefly. When you said a military ID card, do you recall when you received that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall, but I know we had a military ID card, and I have kept mine. I still have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate, year, month even?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember, but it may not have been right at the beginning. However, I can't remember the date. It's probably on the ID itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have an ID card from the JNA, from your time in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What did you do with that card, if anything at all?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When we were leaving the JNA, we were duty-bound to return the ID card to the unit that had issued it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You also mentioned a gun. Do you recall when you received the gun?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I received weapons when I reported to this brigade in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And again I'll ask you the same question. Did you have a gun from your time in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, while I was in the JNA I had both a gun and a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What did you do with those, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: We returned those weapons to the JNA units we had served in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I gave back my weapons when I set out to join the unit in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Let me go back for a second and ask that same question with regard to the ID card. When did you give back the ID card? The JNA ID card, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely what time or what date it was, but as my home unit was in Uzice and I had family in Uzice, I think that on my first visit to my family after my stay in Bosanska Krupa I reported to my unit in Uzice, formally informed them I was staying on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that on that occasion I gave back my military ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If I could have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in Han Pijesak until November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then, a new corps was formed within the Army of Republika Srpska. It was called the Drina Corps, and I was appointed battalion commander -- signals battalion commander, that is, in that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The corps commander appointed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: General Milenko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Where was the -- the signals battalion, where was that located?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was within the corps command at Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How large was the signals battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The battalion at the outset had about 20 privates and three or four officers, and by the end of the war it had grown to between 60 and 70 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How large is a battalion if it is fully staffed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: About 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You said by the end of the war it had grown to between 60 and 70. At any point in time was it larger than that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How was your signals battalion organised?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which had the 67th Regiment for communications, we were given some 20 men and the minimum quantity of technical equipment we needed to establish communications with subordinate units and the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Let's spend a moment there. You said to establish communication with subordinate units in the superior command. What were the duties, the obligations, of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My task was to establish and maintain communications with the superior command and the subordinate units based on the plans drawn up by the signals chief of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to the plans in a little bit. The -- if we could focus on the Drina Corps for a second. What unit -- what army was the Drina Corps part of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps was part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who was the Drina Corps subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was directly subordinated to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, who was that subordinated to, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was subordinated to the Presidency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long were you in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the time until the beginning of February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And at that point in time, had the war ended?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the war was over by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just quickly summarise your positions and your roles after February of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: From that time, for a year, I was the commander of the infantry brigade in Sekovici, which was part of the Drina Corps and later on the 3rd Corps of the VRS. After that, I was chief of signals of the 5th Corps of the VRS. After that, I was commander of the infantry brigade in Visegrad of the VRS. Then I was sent by the VRS for training in the Army of Yugoslavia, the General Staff school, for a year. On my return from that school, I again took up duties in the VRS and I was commander of the brigade in Visegrad again. Then I was chief of the department for morale, information, legal and religious affairs in the Army of Republika Srpska in the 5th Corps, and that was the end of my professional career.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Well, you say that was the end of your professional career. Did you retire or you pensioned off? What do you mean that that was the end of your professional career?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I retired, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What army did you retire from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could just go back in time for a minute. You referred to completing the General Staff academy in 1999. Was that your first time at the General Staff academy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time I had attended that academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Was there a time previously that you had applied to the academy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Can you just give us some of the circumstances, explain to us what happened? And actually, let me clarify so you have a little idea of where I'm going. Did you attend the academy in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I was admitted, but I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who admitted you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia because I applied to go to that school or academy as one of the conditions facilitating admission was that officers who had the rank of captain and who had had an average grade of over 9 in their previous schooling could be admitted. I took advantage of that and I was admitted in 1994 as the first, top of the list of candidates admitted. So when the decision of the chief of the personnel administration [Realtime transcript read in error "admission"] of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia arrived saying that I should be relieved of my duty and sent for schooling at the academy, in the Main Staff of the VRS they did not approve this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Hold on. Let's break this down a little bit. You said the decision of the chief of the personnel -- it says "admission," I believe that should be "administration" arrived. Was that an oral decision or a written decision?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a written order that I should be relieved of my duty as commander of the signals battalion of the VRS in Vlasenica and that I should be sent for schooling. When the personnel council in the Main Staff of the VRS considered that decision, General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Before we get there, before we get there. Was that document signed, the decision that you received, was that signed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to see the order; however, all orders of that kind have to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. I cut you off there. You started to say the personnel council of the Main Staff. Could you explain what that is? Sorry, the personnel council of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is a body in the Army of Republika Srpska that consists of the commander of the Main Staff, with his assistant commanders, and the commanders of the corps. They discuss all important matters related to personnel in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. So they received your -- they received the decision regarding your admission to the school -- the General Staff academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What was their role in the decision, meaning? Why did they receive it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Because they were the ones in charge of implementing that order later and relieving me of my duty and thereby permitting me to go to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After returning from the personnel council, General Zivanovic, corps commander, invited me to come to his office. He told me that that order had arrived, that they discussed it, that General Mladic was very surprised, that he literally tore up the order and said, Tell Jevdjevic that he will go to school when the war is over and when I personally send him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to a different topic. I want to discuss your leaving the JNA. You mentioned that you gave back your gun, your card. What did that mean for you? What was the effect of giving those items back?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: For me personally this meant that in that way my status in the Yugoslav People's Army was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the 30th Personnel Centre during the time-period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: During the second half of the war, I was familiar with it; during the first half, I did not know about it. But during the second half, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: During the second half, could you be more specific? When did you first hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And did you see any sort of documentation? Did you receive anything? How did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that this was an administrative department that was in charge of dealing with administrative matters related to professional officers in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: My question was actually if you received anything. Did you receive any sort of documentation? How did you actually find out about the existence of the personnel centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any documents whatsoever. I just heard that this existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go back to the answer that you just gave, that in a your understanding this was an administrative department in charge of dealing with administrative matters. Could you be more specific? What sort of administrative matters did you understand the personnel centre to be dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I meant that they deal with administrative matters related to status, specifically my own status, that this was a way in which I could receive a salary and other income that was due to professional officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Let's spend a moment on your salary. Who did you receive your salary from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I received my salary the same way all the time from the moment I joined the Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say, it was paid into my current account with the post office bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Where was that account located?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was opened in the post office bank of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time that you were not being paid?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall why you were not being paid?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was a consequence of certain political pressures between Belgrade and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And are you aware how long this consequence of certain political pressures went on?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Six months -- I don't know actually about the consequences, but I know that I did not receive my salary for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer to a better question. So you were not paid for six months. That's what you've just said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you receive any sort of compensation during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Not in terms of money, but we received some kind of compensation from the Army of Republika Srpska. Like all other fighting men, we received food supplies and other things that our families needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What sort of food supplies and other things for the family are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Flour, sugar, cooking oil, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You said "our families." Did you receive this, or did your families receive it? Who received these -- the food supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: We in the Army of Republika Srpska received that, and we could send it to our families that lived either in the territory of Republika Srpska or in the territory of Serbia, specifically my family at that point in time lived in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, were you promoted in the VRS at all during your time of service?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How many times were you promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Twice. It was a fast-track promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with the first one. Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And what rank were you promoted to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Let's talk about what the effect of a promotion is. What actually happens when you get promoted? I mean, are there benefits that go along with being promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: One of the basic benefits was that on the basis of higher rank one received a bigger salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And when you were promoted in 1993 to captain first class, did you receive a higher salary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during a certain period of time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What do you mean by a certain period of time? Does it happen immediately? Is there a time lag?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Once we would be promoted to a higher rank in the Army of Republika Srpska, then our personnel organs from the corps to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska would send information to that effect to the 30th Personnel Centre. It was only when conditions were met within the Army of Yugoslavia for early promotion, that rank would be recognised by them and, accordingly, they would raise our salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I don't believe you've actually answered my question. I was asking if there is -- when the change in pay actually took place regarding the 1993 promotion.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were there any other changes that took place? Was there any other -- within the VRS, were there any other consequences as a result of your -- the promotion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: That's fair. Let's actually move on to the second promotion. When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: 1994. That's when I was promoted to the rank of major of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And again, did a higher salary come with the promotion and rank?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the 30th Personnel Centre, that rank was verified for me only in June 1995 in accordance with their regulations. So it is only from that moment onwards that I was entitled to a higher salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Could you be more specific about when your promotion in the VRS took place. You said 1994. Was there a month that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a new topic. Throughout your testimony you've talked about signals or communications. Did you specialise in anything when you were at the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was the signals department of the military academy that I graduated from, so I'm a specialist in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Is it safe to say that through all of your postings within the VRS that you -- and the JNA that you were in a signals unit or battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, up until February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Currently I work at the Telekom of Srpska as an engineer in maintaining basic stations for mobile telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How long have you worked at Telekom?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's been almost nine years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Have you received any other specialised training or education with respect to communications?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I would be moving on to a new topic now, so I was wondering if this would be a convenient time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is convenient to you, Mr. Mair, we will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I would just like to go back briefly on one topic I forgot to ask a question before. At page 23, line 24 of today's transcript, you referred to receiving money at your bank account in Serbia. Who received the money? Who went and picked up the money when it was deposited into that account?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: My family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Was that throughout the war that your family picked it up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's the way it was throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on now to communications systems. Speaking generally in a broad sense, could you describe how the JNA communications system operated, how it worked?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA had its own General Staff, and large formations were subordinated to it. In my day it was the so-called military districts. Then the General Staff had direct communication with all these military districts. They, in turn, had direct communications with their subordinated units, and that is how the vertical line went down all the way to the lowest ranking units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And the communications from the General Staff to the military district, how did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: From a technical point of view, that took place through stationary communications centres and stationary communications nodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What's the difference between a communication centre and a communication node?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Stationary communications centres were located in towns where JNA units were stationed. Usually these were bigger buildings that had stationary equipment. They were linked up, and they could thereby ensure the necessary communications for certain JNA units. Stationary communications nodes were primarily located on elevations, mountaintops. For them it was indispensable to have proper visibility, thereby having proper communication with various JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on the last sentence there, that it was indispensable to have proper visibility. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because there is equipment, there are the so-called radio relay equipment pieces which basically require optical visibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What happens if there is no optical visibility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then it was not possible to communicate along those lines, then other solutions had to be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could just spend a moment here on the radio relay communications and connections. How does that actually work, briefly, for us who may not be -- may not be as well aware as how these communications systems work?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Radio relay communications are channelled radio communications, as it were. That is to say that if two points anywhere on the ground wish to communicate, there has to be optical visibility between the two. The basic feature of radio relay communications is the fact that transmitter and receiver antennae have to face each other, look at each other, as it were, so that there could be communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Is there any sort of distance limitation? What sort of distance -- when you say that they have to be facing each other, is there a particular range that has to be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The prescribed range for radio relay equipment that we had is 50 kilometres at an optimum. However, if weather conditions were good and if the equipment involved performs well, then the distance could be increased up to, say, 80 or 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If you know, across the territory of the former Republic of Yugoslavia, meaning SFRY, how many of these communication nodes were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that point in time, there were a great many stationary communications nodes. In my view, in my assessment, it was, say, 30 or 40, but I wouldn't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did these communication nodes require personnel to be on location?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was a permanent crew there all the time with at least one officer or one NCO and several soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What about the communications centres, do you know approximately how many of those were on the territory of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few of them as well. I assumed that there were more of them than stationary communication nodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Why would you assume that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Because there were quite a few garrisons of the JNA and every one of these garrisons of the Yugoslav People's Army is a unit that is located basically in that garrison, and every such unit had its own communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How many people would be within the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the stationary communications centre, depending on its size and purpose, there would be 10 to 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And how would that be organised? How would the communications centre operate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: All kinds of indispensable communications are brought together within a communications centre, and then there is commutation within that centre in order to meet the needs of certain commands and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Could you explain the term "commutation," please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In stationary communications centres there was equipment that would relay certain communications, and there would be switchboards for switching, as it were, lines and communications. That is what switchboards are for, exchanges. Then also there were teleprinters for sending and receiving coded messages. Also there was personnel that was there to service all that technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: So thus far I think we've just been talking about radio relay communication. Were there any other sorts of communications being used during the time of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Yugoslav People's Army, radio communications were used also, then wire communications, signal communications, and courier communications. That is the division according to type.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take those one at a time starting first with the radio communications. Can you explain to us -- first, if you could just explain how radio communications work.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Radio communications have certain -- special characteristics. Electro-magnetic waves from antennae and radio equipment spread radially in all directions. In order to have that kind of communication, it is not indispensable to have optical visibility. In radio communications, different kinds of equipment are used, depending on the wishes of the organisers, depending on the range that they wish to have. They are very sensitive communications. They are prone to intercepts. For the most part, they are used only when absolutely necessary and at lower tactical levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You just said that they were used only when absolutely necessary. Was there any sort of policy in place? Was there any reason that they were only used when absolutely necessary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only in cases when there was an interruption and other kinds of communications failed. I'm referring primarily to radio relay and wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the wire communications. Again, can you explain briefly how -- how wire communications worked.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Wire communications are something most people probably understand best. There are permanent cables above and below ground or on posts. So the signal travels through a wire or a cable which can be placed either below or above ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What was the wire communications system like in the former -- in SFRY -- on the territory of the SFRY? What -- how developed was it? What was the communications system like?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In an earlier period of time, wire communications in the JNA were quite important because in that period telecommunications technology for radio relay and stationary communications, optical cables, and so on, had not been developed to a great extent. So that there were wooden posts supporting cables like the public telephone system operated by the PTT, the post office company. And these communications were used for the needs of the JNA. Some 40 years ago the JNA embarked on a large-scale project and placed a large telephone cable underground, running through the central part of Yugoslavia. It was called the central. And it was used to establish and maintain certain communications between units and commands, but it was also used for civilian purposes in parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: The central, as you called it, what did that run between? What were the locations covered by that cable?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It connected points from Ljubljana through Zagreb, Bihac, Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Uzice, all the way to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Was the central operational throughout the war for all of those points?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I know about the area of responsibility stretching from Sarajevo, that is, the Drina Corps where I was throughout the war and where I was the commander of the signals battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you talk about the area of responsibility stretching from Sarajevo, more specifically, what points that you referred to previously would be covered by this stretch of the central?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know about the condition of that cable and the fact that it was technically not in good order on the stretch from Sarajevo to Visegrad, the Drina. So I know about the condition of that cable on that stretch in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You said it was technically not in good order. What does that mean? What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in the village of Pesurici, in the spring of 1992 - and this is between Rogatica and Visegrad - there was a sabotage carried out by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the cable was dug up and cut off. On another spot near Visegrad, some sort of earth-moving equipment that was being used to construct a road cut off that cable as well so that it stopped operating, and it is not operational yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were any attempts made to fix the cable?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of discussion about that. A lot of ideas were put forward because we were forced to organise other kinds of communications with all the units in that area. I'm referring primarily to radio relay communications. But in the course of the war, we did not have the spare parts we needed, the cables, the parts used to join parts together and so on. It had to be constantly in a vacuum. It had to be free of moisture so that when the cable was cut water seeped into it and poured down the cable for some 100 metres causing a short circuit. So it would not have been rational to try and fix it without the proper spare parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were -- the portion going from Sarajevo towards Visegrad, that there were two points on that line that were cut. Where does that line continue on to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That underground cable went on from Visegrad towards the border with what is today Serbia, to Uzice, and then via Cacak to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. What was the effect of the wire being cut in two places on the wire communications system on the territory of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The consequences were such that due to the cable being cut both the army which had used that cable and the civilian structures that had used it were unable to use it for communication purposes. They had to seek other technical solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thus far we've just been talking about the underground cable. Were there other sorts of cable that were in use?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were permanent wires supported by posts, but this technology was already becoming outdated, both for civilian purposes and for military purposes. There were other kinds of communications that supplanted those, so that when the VRS was formed in the Drina Corps - and I assume also on the territory of other units - we did not have nor did we ever draw up a plan for setting up these permanent cable communications supported on posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I believe the next type of communication that you mentioned was signals communication. What does that entail?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Signals communications are communications of a limited character used mostly in smaller units, primarily tank units or in the navy when little flags and hand movements are used to send signals across a short distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And the last type of communication you mentioned was courier. What does that entail?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Courier communications, to put it simply, mean carrying certain oral or written information by a courier who can move on foot, on a motorcycle, or in a motor vehicle. Courier communications may be considered to be the safest kind of communication, but we used them only for messages that were not urgent and for telegrams or other documents which had many typed pages or for instructions that were not urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony you discussed the JNA withdrawal first from Croatia and then from Bosnia. When the JNA withdrew from the territory of Bosnia, did they take anything with them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they took with them their technical equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Regarding the communications system that was in place in Bosnia, did they take any part of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took, in my estimation, the best technical equipment, but some technical equipment did remain on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was used by all three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: First let's talk about the technical equipment they took. You said it was the best. Can you be more specific? What types of equipment did they take?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA was equipped with quite up-to-date equipment for radio relay communications, for telephone communications, and for encryption devices so that the devices that were most important to ensure secure, good-quality, and reliable communications between operative units were taken back to Yugoslavia by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: You also mentioned that all three armies took over parts that remained. First, what three armies are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the VRS, the BH army, which consisted of two components, the HVO, and the Muslim component. So those are the three armies I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And just so I understand your answer, you're dividing the BH army into two, the HVO and the Muslim component. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you saying that those were separate armies or what are you -- how do you get to three armies from that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all these three armies fought among themselves on many -- in many theatres. The VRS fought both the Muslim army and the HVO, the Muslim army fought both the HVO and even their own Muslim army on the territory of Cazinska Krajina. That's why I say what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you say the "Muslim army," did that army have a name?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Both the Muslim army and the HVO together made up the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were the two components of the BH army, but those two components fought one another. They were mutually opposed in many places and at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. What sort of -- you said that there was certain materials that remained that the three armies took over. How did that occur? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: After the withdrawal of certain JNA units, parts of their equipment stayed behind. Whether this was something that had been agreed on, whether the equipment had been captured, or whatever. Some of that equipment came from the Territorial Defence staffs, which together with the JNA had made up the armed forces of Yugoslavia, so that some communications equipment remained behind, both belonging to the JNA and belonging to the Territorial Defence. And that was the equipment we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Remained behind where? Where was this material located?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The material was in depots of the Territorial Defence or, quite simply, in the barracks that were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And so how was the material divided up? Was there some sort of agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. So how was the material divided up? How did the VRS come upon that equipment which it obtained?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the Territorial Defence staffs, it took equipment from the Territorial Defence depots which it could place under its control when the war broke out. Some equipment they obtained from units of the JNA which were withdrawing to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What type of equipment was the VRS -- did it take from these Territorial Defence depots?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Most probably it took weapons and other technical communications equipment which was in those Territorial Defence depots, but the quality of that equipment was far lower than the quality that the JNA had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: So what was the effect of the JNA withdrawal on the communications infrastructure left in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The effect was such that, quite simply, by withdrawing, the JNA withdrew its entire communications system, both as regards technical equipment and organisation and plans. The communications system that had previously existed on that territory was, quite simply, no longer in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: So what did that mean for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It meant that the VRS had enormous problems because the system had been disrupted to such an extent that the VRS had to set up its own communications system with the equipment it had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could call up P149 on the screen. And, Your Honour, we have a binder prepared for the witness. I believe the Prosecution has reviewed it and accepts it. If that could be handed over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Show it to the witness. They must see that one that you are giving to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I believe there are two English translations in e-court. If we could have the first one, 0060-7339 ET-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jevdjevic, if you could please turn to tab 24 in your binder. This is the analysis of the combat-readiness and activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992. Mr. Jevdjevic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And we can see that it was -- a little bit down it says Han Pijesak April 1993. Were you aware that this document was created at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 31 in the English and page 29 in the B/C/S, and I believe that it will be page number 29 for you, Mr. Jevdjevic. And you can see -- in the English version there are two boxes on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could actually scroll down a little bit. I'd like to refer to the the first paragraph after the second box. It starts with stationary wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jevdjevic, that would be the first paragraph below the figure for you. If I could read the second sentence, it says: "Overall, we had a rather well developed aerial wire network of about 95.000 kilometres as well as a somewhat less developed cable network, especially in the hilly and mountainous regions of former BH. However, the use of that kind of communications in the zone of the former JNA was very limited and in certain areas ... impossible." Mr. Jevdjevic, do you have any comment on that sentence -- those two sentences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Jevdjevic answers, Your Honours, he's pointed out that he's not aware of this document, he's not seen it before. I have no difficulty him commenting on parts of the document, but he would need to know the context in which this remark is being made, what area does it refer to, what period does it refer to, perhaps who made the statement and for what purpose. At the moment, Your Honours, any answer that he can give is of no assistance without more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: That's not a problem. If we could just go back a few pages in e-court. It would be page 30 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S, I believe. Forward a page in the B/C/S I think, page 29 -- no, 27. Sorry, wrong direction. Yes. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we see at the top there it says: "1.1.6.2 Conditions under which the communications system of the Army of RS was developed in 1992." Do you see that, Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If you go to the second paragraph there, it says: "Disrupted from the very beginning of the war and increasingly as it gained momentum, the stationary part of the communications system of the former JNA and the communications of other operators (PTT, Ministry of Interior, television, radio, power generation, and distribution enterprises, and railways) as well as the power generation and transmission systems suffered major damage, and part of the war weaponry and equipment of the communication corps was left in the territory of the opponent." Does that accord with what you were just referring to a few minutes ago about the withdrawal of the JNA and that communication equipment which was taken and left?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that satisfies Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, now we understand the context in which he was answering the question. I have no further comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we could go back to the -- page 29 in the B/C/S, 31 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And if you could answer the question that was posed before, and I can repeat it to you if you've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you will, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I had read to you the last two sentences of the first paragraph after the figure beginning: "Stationary wire communications ..." And actually I believe I just asked you to comment on those sentences.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This corresponds to what we have just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have a little point for you to clarify for me here, sir. When you explained the various communications systems, radio, wire, signal, courier, you described wire as a system that uses cable, telephone wires. Now, this paragraph talks of a well developed aerial wire network and a somewhat less developed cable network, suggesting that these are two separate networks. Your explanation suggested that this is one and the same network. Can we explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you able to answer His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Cable lines and aerial lines in military terminology are considered to be wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: So cable communications is a subpart of the wire communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Even the man in the street knows that both are essentially wires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, and that's why you made -- you explained them as one and the same thing. You said cable and wire are one and the same thing. Now, I don't understand what you mean that cable is subpart of wire. You see, what is said here is different from what you explained to us a little earlier when you explained what you called wire communications system. When you did explain that, you said wire communications system is a system that uses cables, and therefore, lay as I am, I was left with the impression that wire and cable are used interchangeably to describe one and the same thing. Now this paragraph separates the two and suggests that there is wire on the one hand and there is cable on the other hand. Now, I'm just asking -- or I see you shaking your head. Maybe you can explain. You just clarify me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, Your Honour. This chief of communications of the Main Staff who compiled this report starts with this paragraph with the following wording: "Stationary wire communications ..." So it is stationary wire communications, and further down he subdivides them into cable and wire networks. For everyone that means that permanent aerial lines and cable lines are both wire communications. If you have the translation, you will see here that he is referring to these subtypes of wire communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see there is an addition of the word "aerial" to the wire network. Do I understand that the wire network is the one that goes on telephone poles and the cable is the one that goes underground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if we could move two paragraphs down, it says -- actually, before we do that, if we could just go to the next paragraph which says that: "This represented a major problem in the planning and organising of this type of communications in the zone of the Army of Republika Srpska, and especially at the corps-brigade level." Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because these stationary aerial wire lines -- well, this analyst speaks about them in the past tense and says "we had" such and such, which means that already by the time the war started they could not be used, both due to damage and their lack of functionality. Therefore, further down he says that this was one of the major problems in the organisation and planning of these communications, and we did not have at corps or brigade level or some other levels this type of communications as had been planned because they had been disrupted, it was very difficult to maintain them, they went along poles from one city to another. It had to do with copper wire which was often stolen. Also it was difficult to maintain when it snowed. So throughout the war, we could not count on this type of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And to now go down to the next paragraph which says: "Reconstruction of this network would be unprofitable. It is susceptible to interference and countermeasures, and its functionality in this war is limited." Do you know if that position ever changed during the period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It did not change during the course of the conflict. I personally tried to get this kind of communication working, aerial communication, between Vlasenica and Han Pijesak.
