I personally tried to repair that. It functioned only for a month. But then again it was damaged when it snowed. The cables and the wires were cut by motor saws by certain individuals who wanted to use them, civilians, and therefore the army thought that this was not a viable way of working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could move forward in the document to page 40 in the English and page 36 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: This is a topic we will go into a little bit further down the line, but I just wanted to pause on it while we're in the middle of this document. If we could focus on the middle of the page, I believe, in both 1.1.6.5. And number 1 there refers to the: "... revival and continuation of manufacture of communications equipment and crypto-protection apparatuses for their repair in the Rudi Cajevac electronics and telecommunications factory in Banja Luka." Are you familiar with that factory?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What sort of factory was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a factory that functioned within the military industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you say the military industry, are you referring to the special purpose industry?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to special purpose industry. This was electronics; it had to do with the manufacture of electronics equipment and communications equipment for the needs of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Who controlled that factory, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of the former JNA. As the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew, it was under the control of the Ministry of Defence of the army -- of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could go forward one more page in each English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And just above 1.1.7, two lines above that, it says: "I judge the combat-readiness of the signals system and corps for 1992 to have been very good. "I propose that this grading be adopted." Mr. Jevdjevic, do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: This grade was presented by the signals chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I was at a far lower level, and I therefore cannot comment on this grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I don't need that document anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, you've talked about the condition of communications system in the VRS. Was it necessary then for the VRS to accumulate additional communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And why did they have to do that again? If you could just be a little bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Because we did not have the right amount of such equipment. What we had barely made it possible to carry out planned communications, but at a significantly decreased capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: How did the VRS go about obtaining -- actually, before we go there. Did the VRS obtain additional equipment, communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the procedure in terms of looking for the kind of equipment that we needed was as follows: We always turned to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: My question was actually if the VRS obtained any additional equipment. Do you know if that -- if they did during the period of the conflict? We'll limit it to your time-period in the Drina Corps, from 1992 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout my stay in the Drina Corps, we got a negligibly small amount of communications equipment from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. For part of the equipment, we made do on our own. We bought some in the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If we could spend a moment on that last sentence. You first say "we." Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, then I don't understand you, sir. Your full answer at line 15 says: "Throughout my stay in the Drina Corps, we got a negligibly small amount of communications equipment from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. For part of the equipment, we made do on our own. We bought some in the market." Now, when you say "we," refers to Republic of -- the Army of Republika Srpska, then I don't understand why in the previous answer you separated the Republika Srpska army from the "we."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider myself to be a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. I was referring to myself, that is, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Go on, Mr. Mair. I don't think it will serve any purpose to pursue this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Perhaps if we clarified the market that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: All our brigades were primarily established in the territory of towns. We as an army had a very modest system of supplies on all grounds. Therefore, the business community of that particular town would organise itself to buy on their own for the soldiers of those units in that town uniforms, fuel, cigarettes, et cetera. Among other things, they would also buy some communications equipment. That's what I actually meant when I was saying "we." I meant brigades, I meant the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they buy anything else, these business people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I can tell you exactly which factories in Vlasenica and in the other towns where I was. They bought for us the following: Motorolas, communications equipment that were sold in the free market. These are not classical military equipment, but they're very good for communications. They also bought cables for us, for field telephones. From various companies we received their switchboards that were in their buildings, and then we used these switchboards for military purposes. So that's the kind of thing I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated that they also bought uniforms for you. My question is: Apart from communications equipment, did they buy you anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a signalsman and that is what mattered the most as far as I was concerned. And that is what I know the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know what mattered to you. If you do know if they bought you anything else, you can tell us, even though it didn't matter to you. The question to you is: Do you know if they did buy you anything else outside uniforms and telecommunications systems? Whether it mattered to you or not is not important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sir. Yes, Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were there any other sources of communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were the sources for the most part; generators, Motorolas, cables, switchboards, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Sorry, my question was not clear. Were there any other persons or entities or organisations from which the VRS or, more specifically, the Drina Corps received communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps, specifically I, also received part of our equipment from the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Anyone else from which you received communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you know if the VRS received communications equipment from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before Mr. Jevdjevic can answer the question, I think you need to state the grounds upon which he can answer that question. He's already answered on the basis of his position within the Drina Corps, what the Drina Corps could receive. If he's being asked about what other units or other parts of the army received, a foundation would need to be laid for that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Perhaps I've been hasty, sir. I see from the transcript that he actually did answer the question. He can't shed any light on it. I can withdraw my objection and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did he answer your question, sir -- where did he answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: At line 10, sir. Just as I was objecting, he answered "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Mair, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, if you know, what was the relationship of the VRS communications system to the VJ communications system?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move on to talking about communications plans. First, was there a general communications plan for the army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you aware -- how often was that -- actually. Who drafted that plan, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Communications plan for the Army of Republika Srpska was drafted by the signals chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Radenko Prole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Did you see that plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you aware of when the plan was drafted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Was it updated throughout the war, or did the same plan remain as it was when it was drafted, as you say, immediately when the war started?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: It remained the same, basically. Like at the beginning of the war, it was just updated when a new unit would be established within the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were you aware of the contents of the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just aware of the excerpt of the plan that pertained to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What sort of information would that excerpt contain?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That excerpt included several orders and several documents from the communications plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: What sort of orders are these -- are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps received an order for communications containing basic information about how, when, and where communications should be established between the Drina Corps and the Main Staff and how the Drina Corps could establish communication with its subordinate units. That order was accompanied by a few other documents and schematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Your answer -- previously you referred to several documents from the communications plan. Is that what you're -- just now referred to when you talked about accompanied by a few other documents and schematics or was there more to the plan than that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: That order for communications and these documents comprise that plan of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Were there any other communications plans in addition to the general communications plan that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: If there was an operation or some sort of exercise to take place, would there be a plan created for that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: For particular operations, every unit and command carrying out that particular operation would create a separate plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Can you just walk us quickly through how that plan would be created. How would that originate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: If a particular operation were to take place, specifically in the area of responsibility of a corps, then the signals chief or communications chief of that corps would turn to the commander and the Chief of Staff of the corps from whom he would receive specific information as to which units participate, where the combat operations would take place, where the command posts of these units would be, and other such information. On the basis of that information received, the signals chief of the corps would create a mini plan, if I can call it that way, for that operation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And again, just to make sure we're using the same language, you said the signals chief of the corps would create a mini plan. Are we referring to communications or just signals, the signals communications that you were referring to earlier when we talked about the types of communications?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: He would create a mini plan of communications only for carrying out that particular operation in that locality, and that plan of communications is null and void once that operation is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Generally speaking, what sort of communications -- what types of communications may be involved in the mini plan that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Most frequently in such mini plans we used short-wave radio communications to communicate with subordinate units and one channel of radio relay communications in order to communicate with the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. And once that mini plan is created, what happens after that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: When the mini plan is drawn up, the chief of communications on orders from the corps commander would give the plan to me as the commander of the communications battalion in order for me to carry out the plan. An excerpt from the same plan would be given to all the subordinate units participating in carrying out the task so that we could all communicate with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: When you say that the chief of communications would give the plan to you, are you referring to only the mini plan, the communications plan, or would you receive the entire plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Only the mini plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You note the time. Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, have you ever heard of something called the Drina Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any documents related to the Drina plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: During the period of the conflict, did you ever hear any sort of information about something called the Drina plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I would like to briefly go back to one topic that we discussed earlier which was your going to school at the General Staff academy. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Could you remind us again when you attended the academy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: From September 1998 to August 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: At that time, were there other members of the VRS that attended schools or academies outside of the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you aware of what some of those -- or where some of those schools or academies were located?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Some of us completed schools and academies in Belgrade, in Serbia, and some colleagues of mine from the VRS completed certain schools in Greece and in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other locations where VRS members attended schools?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know of such locations because I know colleagues who went to school in those countries. There may have been others, but I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to move to our last topic. Have you ever met General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Have you ever had a -- the opportunity to talk with Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was -- excuse me. How many times did you have the opportunity to talk with Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: Once on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In April 1994, or rather, in the spring of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Can you give us some of the circumstances around that phone call. How did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that period, the VRS was engaged in an offensive operation on the forces of the BH army in the area of Gorazde. Some 15 days of fighting ensued under the direct command of General Mladic, and then the units of the VRS managed to crush the BH forces, resisting them, and entered the town of Gorazde. At that time, I was the communications man at the forward command post of the Drina Corps in Rogatica. At one point in time, the telephone rang; they were calling from the Main Staff. As General Mladic was not there and they were looking for him, I said that he was somewhere at the front line and that I did not have any communications with him because he never carried communications equipment with him. They told me there was something important that had to be conveyed to him regarding the political situation and political pressures from the FRY, for that operation to be stopped, and for the VRS to be prevented from entering the town of Gorazde. Half an hour later, the telephone rang. I answered. It was someone from the office of Slobodan Milosevic, the President of Yugoslavia. They were asking for General Mladic. I understood that this was a very urgent and important matter, but I was unable to help them establish communication with him because he was somewhere at the front line. And that's what I told them. I said it was impossible to reach General Mladic. Sometime later, the telephone rang again, and I was surprised when General Perisic introduced himself. He asked who he was talking to, and I introduced myself. He asked whether General Mladic was there, and I said the same thing to him I had told all the others. He then spoke in a tone of entreaty, asking me to try to reach General Mladic by any kind of communication I could and to tell him that General Perisic was under strong pressure from the political leadership of Yugoslavia and that I should convey to him that he should establish contact. He wanted -- or rather, Perisic wanted to establish contact with Mladic and ask him to stop the offensive activities of the VRS. I promised him I would do my best to reach General Mladic. In the evening when General Mladic turned up at the forward command post, I conveyed to him the contents of all these conversations. And he simply said to me, If any of them calls again, tell them you didn't find me. That was my only conversation with General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, I'd like to thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAIR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time. I believe Mr. Thomas has a submission which I don't have any problem with, but he can probably explain it better than I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My request, Your Honours, is that we adjourn and begin the cross-examination tomorrow morning. I appreciate that there's still plenty of time left in the session, but there are a number of documents related to the cross-examination and Mr. Jevdjevic upon which we're still awaiting translations. It's a matter that I need to resolve obviously before I cross-examine, but also for the Defence to be able to make sense of the disclosure that I've provided to them in preparation for Mr. Jevdjevic's testimony. There isn't, unfortunately, a discrete topic that I can deal with with a complete range of translations available at the moment, otherwise I would suggest that we could begin and at least get that done. But I'm not in that position, unfortunately. I do believe that I can resolve these matters pretty easily this afternoon with my learned friends, and I think we'll also have a more stream-lined cross-examination tomorrow. I understand there isn't any other witness who's able to testify follow Mr. Jevdjevic tomorrow, so we have the day, and I will easily conclude tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted an assurance on. You will conclude tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I will conclude tomorrow, sir. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we will be able to have time for re-examination and questions from the Bench and questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Understood, Your Honour. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's understood. Sir, we are not able to finish today, but we're not done with you yet. You have to come back tomorrow. But I must warn you that now that you have taken the -- made the declaration and you are already in the witness box, you may not discuss the case with anybody, least of all the lawyers for Mr. Perisic, until you are excused. So we'll come back tomorrow, the 19th, at 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom. Court adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.43 p.m.,
